rationale: Frog-embryo experiments show a neural-plate voltage pattern that alcohol, nicotine, and Notch disruption disturb, and restoring it with an HCN-family channel improves brain anatomy and neural gene expression. Learning recovery is also reported, but it is the weakest arm and morphological rescue is often partial, so the full conjunction is likely rather than certain.

Tumors do lose tissue-scale coordination, but somatic clonal selection and exploitation of shared resources show cancer cells are more selfish at cell level, not merely smaller selves. The cognitive-light-cone redescription is an unmeasured metaphor and does not replace that evolutionary evidence.

Gap junctions close under physiological stress and are often lost early in transformation, and inert smooth implants can induce sarcomas. A positive-feedback loop in which lower connectivity makes local computation easier and thereby drives further uncoupling has not been demonstrated.

In frog embryos, foci expressing human oncogenes show abnormal membrane voltage with voltage-sensitive dyes before a visible mass, so early bioelectric detection holds in that model. The system is a transparent embryo rather than a solid adult tumor, and independent replication is limited.

Transient depolarization of instructor cells together with serotonergic signaling can make frog melanocytes overproliferate and invade without an introduced oncogene or classic carcinogen. The phenotype is fairly called melanoma-like, though it is not mammalian melanoma and not every form of DNA damage was excluded.

Forcing hyperpolarization in frog embryos reduces tumor formation driven by KRAS and other human oncogenes while the oncogene is still expressed, and some existing foci regress. Prevention is better supported than full normalization, and the setting is an embryonic model.

Suppressing an oncogene-driven phenotype in frog embryos does not show that physiological information processing dominates cancer outcomes in animals or humans. Driver mutations, inherited risk, and responses to genetically targeted drugs show that genetic state strongly determines many clinical outcomes.

Large groups of frog embryos are reported to carry a shifted transcriptome and to survive chemical teratogens better than isolated embryos, which shared secreted signals can explain. How large that protection is, and whether the group is a genuine higher-level individual, is not securely established.

The ionophore monensin restores tail outgrowth in tadpoles during the refractory stage, and the same systemic treatment is reported to produce limb-appropriate tissue at leg wounds. That site specificity matches positional identity in the stump; the tail result is firmer than patterned leg regeneration.

Aging is driven by genome damage, epigenetic drift, senescence, and mitochondrial failure, and a causal role for decaying bioelectric anatomical memories is an untested proposal. Partial reprogramming can rejuvenate cells without showing that anti-aging interventions must also restore a bioelectric pattern scaffold.
